source_refs.note: Topic 23.3.2 with Quick Check 23.2, answered (PDF 106-107); the tests are redrawn. The book's HCOONa from acetone is corrected to CH3COONa, and its explanation for ethanol is replaced by oxidation to ethanal. Answers need review.

blocks.text: Aldehydes and ketones are oxidised to carboxylic acids, but aldehydes are oxidised easily while ketones resist oxidation, because a C-C bond would have to be broken. Ketones are oxidised only by strong oxidising agents, while aldehydes are oxidised by both weak and strong ones. Mild oxidising agents therefore tell them apart.

items: Tollens' test: Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate) contains silver ions in aqueous alkaline solution: AgNO3 + 3NH4OH -> [Ag(NH3)2]OH + NH4NO3 + 2H2O. On gentle warming with an aldehyde, the silver ions are reduced to silver metal, forming a silver mirror on the wall of the tube. A dilute solution of glucose (an aldehydic sugar) has been used to make mirrors this way. Ketones do not give this test.

Fehling's test: Fehling's solution is a bright blue solution of Cu2+ ions in aqueous alkali, complexed with a salt of tartaric acid. Warmed with an aldehyde, Cu2+ is reduced to Cu+, which in the alkaline solution forms a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide: RCHO + 2Cu(OH)2 + NaOH -> RCOONa + Cu2O + 3H2O. Ketones do not give this test.

Iodoform test: aldehydes and ketones are readily halogenated at the alpha position. Among aldehydes only ethanal, and among ketones only methyl ketones, contain the CH3CO- (acetyl) group. These react with iodine in sodium hydroxide to form triiodomethane (iodoform), a yellow crystalline solid, so a yellow precipitate shows a CH3CO- group: CH3CHO + 3I2 + 4NaOH -> CHI3 + HCOONa + 3NaI + 3H2O; CH3COCH3 + 3I2 + 4NaOH -> CHI3 + CH3COONa + 3NaI + 3H2O.

blocks.alt: Three test tubes: Tollens' reagent with a silver mirror (aldehydes only); Fehling's solution, blue, with a brick-red Cu2O precipitate (aldehydes only); iodine with NaOH giving a yellow CHI3 precipitate (CH3CO- or CH3CH(OH)- compounds). blocks.long_description: Tollens' and Fehling's reagents are mild oxidising agents: an aldehyde reduces silver(I) to silver metal and copper(II) to red copper(I) oxide, while a ketone does not react. The iodoform test is different: it detects a CH3CO- group (or a CH3CH(OH)- group that can be oxidised to one), whether the compound is an aldehyde, a ketone or an alcohol.

blocks.text: Ethanol also gives the iodoform test, while methanol does not, because ethanol contains the CH3CH(OH)- group, which acts like a methyl ketone structure. In general, alcohols with a CH3CH(OH)- group give the test.

items: Compound A, C3H6O, is reduced by NaBH4 to B, C3H8O. Both give a yellow precipitate with I2/NaOH. Identify A and B.
Why does methanol not give the iodoform test while ethanol does?
Give a different test to distinguish each pair: (i) CH3CH2CHO and CH3COCH3; (ii) CH3CH2COCH2CH3 and CH3CH2CH2COCH3; (iii) CH2=CH-CH2-OH and CH3CH2CHO.
